note: claude-opus-5-5、入力 3163 / 出力 2363 トークン

data.question: Should we loosen the customer contract's pickup_deadline from 120 s to 150 s (option 3), adopt the rule change sanction_lambda 0.5 → 1 instead (option 2), or keep the current v1 rules and contract?
data.background: Option 3 is a contract change that loosens a promise to customers, and customers have no vote, so I must not decide it myself even though all three companies voted for it. Under the KPI and your earlier decision K1, a change worse for customers needs a reason based on its measured effect on p95_wait_s, max_wait_s and unfinished, so you should see those numbers before accepting it. You may also prefer to address blocking through rule changes first. Option 2 is one such rule change, and it passed every machine check.

options.summary: Customers get a looser pickup promise: 150 s instead of 120 s. On-time rises from 121.8 to 122.6 (+0.8) and late falls from 10.4 to 9.6, but only 3/5 seeds improved. Blocked s stays at 2404, road violations stay at 25.8, and p95_wait_s 188, max_wait_s 385 and unfinished 0.0 are all unchanged. The small on-time gain comes from relabeling, because the same waits now count as on time. Actual service is not faster. Lowest on-time rate is 0.85 (from 0.84). Votes are A ○, B ○, C ○.
options.stakeholders: Companies gain slightly: utility A 39.0, B 39.1, C 28.8, against 38.4 / 38.9 / 28.8 now. Customers lose a stronger promise and their actual waits do not improve, so they bear the cost without benefit. Operators gain fewer reported late deliveries but no real service improvement.

options.summary: Rule change; no contract change. On-time rises to 132.2 (+10.4), improving in 5/5 seeds. Late falls to 0.0, blocked s to 845 and road violations to 23.6. Lowest on-time rate is 1.00. p95_wait_s falls to 85.0, max_wait_s falls to 112 and unfinished stays at 0.0. Votes are A ○, B ○, C ×, and it can be adopted automatically.
options.stakeholders: Customers gain under the existing promise: shorter typical and worst-case waits, and no late deliveries. Company A (46.2) and Company B (41.2) gain. Company C loses: its utility falls from 28.8 to 19.2 and it voted against. Fairness between companies is not in the KPI as written (K1), but C's loss is large.

options.summary: Stay at v1. On-time 121.8, late 10.4, blocked s 2404, road violations 25.8, p95_wait_s 188, max_wait_s 385, unfinished 0.0, lowest on-time rate 0.84.
options.stakeholders: No one gains. Customers keep the current promise but continue to see about 10.4 late deliveries and long waits. Company C keeps its current utility of 28.8. A and B forgo the gains they would get under option 2.

recommendation.reason: Option 2 gives the largest on-time gain (+10.4, 5/5 seeds) under the existing promise. It also lowers every customer monitor: p95_wait_s 188 → 85.0 and max_wait_s 385 → 112, with unfinished at 0.0. So no contract loosening is needed. Option 3 makes customers' promise worse while leaving their actual waits unchanged, and its +0.8 gain is weak (3/5 seeds). Under K1 there is no measured customer benefit that would justify it. The main cost of option 2 is Company C's drop in utility (28.8 → 19.2), which you may want to weigh even though fairness is not in the KPI.
assumptions: The 5 measured seeds represent normal demand in the coming period.
Companies will not change their behaviour in ways the simulation does not capture once sanctions are stronger.
Company C's lower utility will not lead it to leave the shared road or reduce its service.

unknowns: How customers perceive a 150 s pickup promise compared with 120 s, and whether a looser promise would affect order volume.
Each company's actual behaviour policy, and whether stronger sanctions would change how they drive beyond what the simulation models.
How Company C will respond to its utility loss under option 2, such as fleet changes or objections.
Next period's demand level and whether these results hold under higher or different load.
Whether options 2 and 3 combined would behave differently; this was not measured.
Effects on customers beyond the measured wait metrics, such as variation by area or by company.
